lead: An operating system serves two groups: people and programs. It gives users a way to start work, run programs, read and write files, talk over a network, and see errors. It also manages shared resources, keeps records, and stops one user from damaging another. These offers are called operating-system services. A phone UPI payment uses many of them in one second. The idea matters because services are the visible face of the kernel; system calls, studied next, are how programs ask for them.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for the resource-manager view and Chapter 1.4 for dual mode, because services must cross the user–kernel boundary safely.

blocks.text: An operating system offers services to the person at the keyboard and to the program that is running. The first user service is the user interface (UI). A command-line interface (CLI) takes typed commands; a graphical user interface (GUI) uses windows, icons and touch. A batch interface reads a file of jobs. The UI is how a user asks for other services.
Program execution loads a program into memory, gives it a process, runs it, and ends it cleanly. The OS must also handle abnormal ends, such as a divide by zero or a missing file.
Input/output (I/O) operations let programs read and write devices. A program should not need device-register details. It asks for a read or write, and the OS and device driver do the hardware work.
File-system manipulation creates, deletes, reads, writes and searches files and directories. It also sets permissions: who may read a salary sheet and who may only see a name.
Communication moves data between processes on one computer or across a network. It can use shared memory or message passing; Unit 2 covers those mechanisms.
Error detection notices CPU and memory faults, device failures, and program errors such as bad addresses or illegal instructions. The OS reports the error and often terminates the program.

Both lists together are titled operating-system services. The first six are the user-facing services; resource allocation, accounting, and protection and security are the system-facing ones. The point is that each service hides hardware detail behind a simple request.

System services keep the whole machine usable, not just one program. Resource allocation decides which process gets the CPU, memory pages, disk bandwidth or a device. When many processes compete, the OS needs policy: first come, priority, fairness. Unit 2 and Unit 4 study CPU and memory allocation.

Accounting records what resources each user or process consumes: CPU seconds, bytes stored, pages printed. A data centre can bill a customer; a university lab can find the heavy user. Accounting is bookkeeping; it does not by itself stop a process.

Protection and security control access. Protection is internal: it stops one process from reading another process's memory or writing a file it does not own. Security defends against outside attackers, such as a stolen password or a network break-in. Chapter 1.4's dual mode is one protection tool; the access matrix and attacks are in Unit 6.

System programs are ready-made programs that sit between raw services and the user. A shell reads commands and starts programs. A file manager shows folders. A compiler turns source into an executable. An editor, backup tool or network utility is also a system program. Most run in user mode and request services through system calls, the subject of Chapter 1.6.
A GUI is a system program too: it draws windows and sends clicks as service requests. The kernel does not need to contain the look of windows; it supplies the services behind them.

A service is a promise; a system call is the door used to ask for it. The service 'read a file' is offered by the OS. The program asks with read(), a system call. The call traps into the kernel and the CPU switches to kernel mode first. The kernel then validates the arguments, runs file-system code, and returns to user mode with a byte count or an error number.

This split matters for design. The service can stay the same while the call changes. A phone OS may offer 'send data' to apps, but one phone may implement it with sockets and another with a message bus. The app still asks for a service.

The split also matters for safety. A user program cannot write disk blocks directly. It must ask the service, and the kernel checks permission. That is why dual mode from Chapter 1.4 exists: the mode bit prevents a user program from pretending to be the OS.

Some services are not system calls in every OS. Accounting may be a background daemon reading kernel counters. A GUI may be a server process. Protection may be checked in the kernel for memory, but a file server may check network permissions. Ask 'who provides the service?' and 'what entry does the program use?' separately.

spec.aria: A tree splits OS services into user services for interface, I/O, files, communication and error handling, and system services for allocation, accounting, protection and security.

examples.question: A UPI payment of ₹500 is handled by a phone app. The OS service times are: user-interface event handling 20 ms; fingerprint read 30 ms; network request and reply 40 ms; writing a payment log to flash 10 ms; three permission checks by protection at 1 ms each; one accounting record 2 ms. (a) Name the OS service for each step. (b) Find the total service time in ms. (c) Find the share of total time that is I/O, where I/O means the fingerprint read, the whole 40 ms network step (treated as hardware transfer for this question) and the log write; accounting is not I/O.
steps: UI step: user-interface service. Time = 20 ms.
Fingerprint step: I/O operation. Time = 30 ms.
Network step: communication service; for this question the whole 40 ms is the hardware transfer, so it counts as I/O. Time = 40 ms.
Log step: file-system manipulation; the flash write is I/O. Time = 10 ms.
examples.answer: The payment uses user-interface, I/O, communication, file-system, protection and accounting services; total service time is 105 ms, of which 80 ms is I/O, so I/O is 76.19% of total.
examples.check:
ui = 20
fingerprint = 30
network = 40
log = 10
checks = 3
per_check = 1
protection = checks * per_check
accounting = 2
total = ui + fingerprint + network + log + protection + accounting
io = fingerprint + network + log
share = io / total * 100
print(float(total))
print(float(io))
print(round(share, 2))

traps: A service is what the OS provides. A system call is the programming entry used to request it; do not treat the two words as the same thing.
Protection is internal access control among processes and users. Security is defence against outside attacks. An answer that swaps them loses marks.
A GUI is one kind of user interface, not the only one. A CLI and a batch interface are also user interfaces.
A network send uses the communication service, and its hardware transfer is also I/O. In a time-sum question, count each measured time once unless the question says otherwise.
Accounting records use; it does not enforce a limit. A quota or scheduler enforces limits.

quiz.q: List the six user services of an operating system.
quiz.a: User interface, program execution, I/O operations, file-system manipulation, communication, error detection.

quiz.q: What does the accounting service record?
quiz.a: It records resource use such as CPU seconds, stored bytes and pages printed, per user or process.

quiz.q: Why is protection called internal and security external?
quiz.a: Protection controls access among processes and users inside the system. Security defends the system against outside attacks such as stolen passwords or network break-ins.

quiz.q: Give one difference between a system service and a system program.
quiz.a: A system service is a function the OS provides, such as allocation. A system program is a user-mode program, such as a shell or compiler, that uses services.

quiz.q: A process uses 25 ms UI, 35 ms disk read, 15 ms network and 5 ms permission check. Find total time and I/O share if disk and network are I/O.
A file server checks 4 permissions at 2 ms each. What is the protection time?
An app writes a payment log by passing a physical flash address to the device. Which OS services fail, and what is the risk?
quiz.a: File-system manipulation, protection and I/O operations fail. The app bypasses permission checks, uses no device driver, and performs the device write itself; it can overwrite another app's data or OS data.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, these services appear as APIs: POSIX calls on Linux and macOS, Android system services, and the Windows API. Cloud platforms turn accounting into metering and protection into identity and access control. Search for 'POSIX system interfaces', 'Android system services' and 'cgroups accounting' to see the same split at scale.
